To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) free thyroxine concentrations may be spuriously elevated in patients with variant albumin or circulating thyroid hormone binding antibody; (ii) the presence of these abnormalities can be confirmed by measurement of total thyroxine and free thyroxine index; and (iii) the presence of a spuriously raised free thyroxine should be suspected when a high free thyroxin is obtained in the presence of a normal thyrotrophin concentration.

the measurement of free thyroxin in serum may give a misleadingly high result in patients with familial dysalbuminaemia hyperthyroxinemia or with circulating thyroid hormone-binding antibodies, leading to inappropriate diagnosis and treatment of patients.

1) Free thyroxine concentrations may be spuriously elevated in the presence of circulating thyroid hormone binding inhibitors or variant albumin; 2) This may lead to misdiagnosis of thyrotoxic patients as hypothyroid or euthyroid; 3) The presence of a thyroid hormone binding inhibitor or variant serum albumin may be suspected when there is an inappropriate elevation of free thyroxin concentration in a euthyroid patient.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms of thyroid hormone transport in the blood and the development of methods to measure free thyroid hormone levels in serum.
the study of the thyroid hormone binding proteins and the development of new techniques for their measurement in serum.
understanding the mechanisms by which thyroxine (T4) is released from its carrier protein, albumin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the free thyroxin assay should be used as a screening test of thyroid function and the TSH assay as a confirmatory test of thyroid function in patients with suspected thyroid disease.
the measurement of free thyroxin in the serum of patients with a normal TSH is not useful in the assessment of thyroid function.
the free thyroxin measurement is not a useful screening test for thyroid disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the measurement of free thyroxin is not as reliable as it is often assumed to be.
free thyroxine concentrations should be used with caution and that thyrotrophin should always be measured in patients in whom there are any doubts about the interpretation of the free thyroxines.

in patients without thyroxine excess a free thyroxine result in excess of the reference interval should always be followed by measurement of TSH and if this is normal then further tests should be performed to exclude the presence of either a variant serum albuminaemia or thyroid hormone binding antibody.
The main takeaway from our work is that
clinicians must always interpret the results of thyroid function tests in the clinical context.
clinicians should be wary of free thyroid hormone assays.
clinicians should be aware of the limitations of the free thyroxin test and that the thyrotrophin test should always be used as a confirmatory measure of thyroid status.
